candidateRows: Science can answer every real question through publicly verifiable methods, whereas religion rests on control, wishful thinking, superstition, and unsupported promises.
This establishes the scientific-materialist case by contrasting science's claimed explanatory reach and corrigible method with religion's alleged lack of evidential reliability.
In the opening substantive exchange, Peter defines the fundamental difference between scientific inquiry and religion and states his broad case for science's sufficiency.
Science explains the material world's operation, but questions of value, purpose, meaning, and Christian historical claims remain outside its proper explanatory scope.
This supplies the central theistic distinction between scientific explanation of material processes and other rational questions concerning meaning, value, purpose, and faith.
Peter's claim that science answers every real question and that religion lacks evidence.
Keith accepts science's power within the material domain while disputing its universal scope and defending compatibility between Christian commitment and scientific practice.
Progress in science steadily removes the need for God by explaining values through evolution and approaching even the origin of the universe without divine intervention.
The move directly supports the proposition's scientific-materialist side by arguing that expanding natural explanation makes the God hypothesis unnecessary across multiple domains.
Asked whether future scientific progress moves humanity toward or away from God, Peter predicts that natural explanations will increasingly displace theological ones.
Understanding how the world works does not determine whether God exists, because a complete account of mechanisms can coexist with an originating and sustaining creator.
This is a direct central rebuttal to explanatory displacement, arguing that scientific mechanism and divine agency address distinguishable questions and therefore need not conflict.
Peter's argument that increasingly complete natural explanations make a creator unnecessary.
Keith responds to the forecast of scientific displacement with an analogy intended to show that knowledge of operation does not settle questions of authorship.
God is an unnecessary and defeatist hypothesis because consciousness, ethics, and the world's other features are wholly attributable to material nature and evolutionary history.
This states the debate's strongest ontological materialism: every relevant phenomenon is materially grounded, leaving divine agency without necessary explanatory work.
Keith's claim that scientific understanding of mechanisms remains compatible with an underpinning creator.
Peter rejects the mechanism-versus-creator distinction and extends material explanation from cosmic origins to consciousness and morality.
Material accounts neither explain why anything exists nor derive moral obligations from evolutionary facts, so scientific description alone cannot ground humane conduct or value.
The move attacks two pillars of materialist sufficiency—origins and ethics—by arguing that causal description leaves both ultimate existence and normative obligation unresolved.
Peter's claim that material nature and evolution exhaustively account for the universe, consciousness, and ethics.
Keith challenges Peter's comprehensive materialism by joining the question of why there is something with the distinction between what evolution produces and how people ought to act.
Early testimony concerning Jesus's resurrection and the transformation of his followers provide historically grounded reasons to treat the Christian claim as evidentially serious.
This supplies the debate's principal positive evidential defense of Christianity rather than relying only on limits to science or criticisms of materialism.
Peter's characterization of resurrection, miracles, and religious traditions as pervasive fake news.
Keith answers the dismissal of resurrection belief by appealing to the early dating of transmitted claims and the subsequent change in the disciples and Christian movement.
Human personhood is more than computational performance because people possess distinctive relational dignity that artificial intelligence cannot replace merely by processing information.
This applies the theistic side's account of personhood and dignity directly to future artificial intelligence, a major technological component of the motion.
In response to a new question about whether artificial intelligence could become human, Keith distinguishes useful machine intelligence from irreducible interpersonal personhood.
Humans are already machines, and advanced artificial intelligences will constitute a new species capable of absorbing, reflecting on, and using information without human evolutionary constraints.
The move directly opposes claims of uniquely nonmechanical personhood and advances a materialist vision of future artificial agents as genuine species rather than mere tools.
Keith's claim that relational human personhood is distinctive and cannot be replaced by artificial intelligence.
Peter counters Keith's personhood distinction by placing both humans and emerging artificial agents within a machine ontology while emphasizing their divergent forms and histories.
Genetic modification can be legitimate healing, but enhancement and unequal access risk commodifying human beings, marginalizing vulnerable people, and undermining equal human worth.
This connects Christian moral commitments to a concrete future technology by distinguishing compassionate treatment from practices that could erode dignity and justice.
Asked whether genetic intervention amounts to playing God, Keith permits therapeutic uses while warning that access, enhancement, and attitudes toward disability create serious ethical risks.
Scientific practice and religious belief are intellectually incompatible because religion relies on superstition and wishful thinking rather than evidence.
This directly advances the central claim that scientific standards displace religion by presenting their respective methods of belief formation as fundamentally incompatible.
Keith's claim that practicing scientists can remain Christians and that religious belief will persist alongside scientific discovery.
After Keith argues that Christianity remains common among scientists, Peter denies that one mind can consistently combine science with religious belief and contrasts evidence with superstition.
A transcendent God outside time can be known only through voluntary divine self-revelation rather than ordinary investigation of created things.
The move supplies the theistic account of how knowledge of a transcendent creator is possible, addressing a foundational epistemic objection to belief in God.
Asked how anyone could know a being existing beyond time, Keith distinguishes God from everything created and says finite minds depend on that being choosing to disclose something.
Science can approach cosmic origins by explaining apparent existence as a separation of balanced opposites whose total remains nothing, without invoking a creator.
This is a direct scientific-materialist account of origins and therefore bears centrally on whether scientific explanation can make a divine creator unnecessary.
The challenge that denying divine creation is itself blind superstition and cannot explain why the universe exists.
Peter concedes that science has not completed its account of origins but argues that balanced physical opposites illustrate how apparent something can emerge while the total remains nothing.
Christian interpretation can adapt to established science because disputed cosmological readings of scripture are not essential commitments of Christian faith.
The move directly rebuts the alleged conflict between Christianity and scientific progress by distinguishing central faith commitments from revisable interpretations of scripture.
Peter's position that adaptable religions merely follow scientific discoveries and will ultimately wither as science becomes dominant.

Keith describes his scientific and Christian development as parallel, then argues that Christians have revised noncentral scriptural interpretations concerning creation, cosmology, and related matters.
Chance variation and natural selection provide a complete biological explanation from early self-replicating chemistry through complex human life.
This supplies the scientific-materialist explanation of biological complexity and expressly argues that evolutionary mechanisms remove any explanatory need for divine creation in biology.

Asked what initiated evolution, Peter answers that chance and natural selection explain biological development, contrasting biology's explanatory resources with physicists' remaining origin questions.
Evolution coherently explains biological diversification, but unresolved origins and dimensions of life beyond material description leave room for theism without using God as a gap filler.
The move defines the debate's principal theistic synthesis: accepting evolutionary science while denying that its material account exhausts origins, meaning, or reality.
Peter's claim that natural selection explains all of biology and makes atheism especially straightforward for a biologist.

Keith praises evolutionary explanation, distinguishes it from the unresolved transition to life, rejects a simple God-of-the-gaps inference, and says material science alone need not require God but does not exhaust life.
Belief in an afterlife lacks evidence and can damage present human flourishing by enabling control, martyrdom, and the sacrifice of earthly aspirations.
This connects scientific evidentialism to the debate's question of hope by arguing both that postmortem claims are unjustified and that they have harmful practical consequences.
Peter compares the afterlife with an unsupported hypothesis, then argues that such belief is not harmless because it can be used to control people and depreciate present life.
Human beings have no cosmic purpose, but they can adopt finite daily purposes and enjoy their chance existence without harming other people.
The move directly addresses whether scientific materialism can account for human purpose, replacing divinely assigned meaning with contingent personal aims and ethical enjoyment.
The religious conception that humans possess a cosmic purpose assigned by God, including glorifying God and making life ultimately worthwhile.
Peter rejects any divinely assigned cosmic role, distinguishes it from ordinary chosen purposes, and describes humans as products of complex chance who should enjoy life without injuring others.
Christian apocalyptic hope calls people to faithful action in every generation rather than supporting predictions that the present moment is uniquely the end time.
This explains how Christian future hope can motivate responsible present conduct, directly bearing on whether religious eschatology undermines or supports human flourishing.
Keith treats Revelation as symbolic literature applicable under oppression in any era, rejects confident end-time dating, and says one should live urgently while still doing today's proper work.
Christian belief has historically encouraged scientific engagement because it affirms the physical world as good and worthy of active investigation and modification.
The move directly counters the claim that God obstructs science by arguing that Christian theology positively motivated empirical investigation of the material world.
Peter's contention that religion arrived before science, forced science to battle the God hypothesis, and would never have arisen had science come first.

Keith contrasts escapist spiritual traditions with Christianity's affirmation of physical reality, arguing that this outlook drove pioneering Western scientists toward practical observation and experiment.
The absence of evidence for foundational supernatural claims and the greater likelihood of mistaken testimony undermine belief in miracles.
This directly attacks the empirical credibility of resurrection, virgin birth, afterlife, and miracles, which are central evidential commitments of Christian theism.
Fox's claim that Christian faith historically motivated scientists to investigate the physical world experimentally.
After Fox links Christian commitment with active empirical investigation, Atkins turns that empirical standard against central supernatural Christian claims.
Treating miracle narratives as allegories may convey lessons about life, but it does not establish that the reported events actually occurred.
The move closes off an interpretive defense of miracle narratives by distinguishing their possible symbolic meaning from their historical reality.
A possible Christian defense that miracle accounts function allegorically to illuminate aspects of human life.
Within his broader rejection of miracles, Atkins considers a less literal Christian interpretation and argues that symbolism cannot establish occurrence.
Miracles lack supporting evidence and, as irreproducible departures from nature, would erode the rational predictability required to understand the world.
This combines an evidential objection with a conceptual argument that supernatural exceptions would undermine stable natural expectations and rational inquiry.
The Christian position that genuine divine miracles can occur as departures from ordinary natural processes.
Atkins supplements his denial of reported miracles with a broader argument connecting reproducible natural order to rational expectations about events.
Weak contemporary healing claims warrant caution, but their failure does not show that miracles never occur, and Christianity centrally affirms Christ's resurrection.
The response preserves the possibility of divine action while identifying the resurrection as Christianity's decisive miracle, directly defending the theistic side.
Atkins's categorical denial of miracles based on absent evidence, unreliable reports, and the regularity of nature.
Fox concedes that many modern miracle and faith-healing claims collapse under examination, yet denies that this justifies universal disbelief in miracles.
